summary: Govind Swamirao Gai (1917–1995) was an epigraphist and scholar of Indology and linguistics. He succeeded Dineschandra Sircar, served as Chief Epigraphist for the Archaeological Survey of India (1966–1976), and was an epigraphy consultant for AIIS in 1986.

Govind Vinayak Devasthali (1906–1996) was an Indologist who studied under Hari Damodar Velankar. He served as Professor of Sanskrit at HPT Arts and RYK Science College (attested 1944) and Professor at Savitribai Phule Pune University (attested 1967–1968).
Govind Vishnu Kathavate was an Indologist who succeeded Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar and held the Sanskrit chair at the Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute.

Govindlal Hargovind Bhatt was an Indologist who taught at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda (attested 1933–1939). He later succeeded Benoytosh Bhattacharyya as Director of the Oriental Institute, Vadodara (attested 1953–1957).

Grace S. Fong (born 1948) is a Sinologist who studied at McGill University and the University of British Columbia. She taught as a Professor at Smith College (~1985–1987) and served as associate professor and department chair at McGill (~1993).

Graeme MacQueen (1948–2023) was a Buddhist studies and religious studies scholar. He completed his doctoral studies at Harvard University (~1974–1979) under Masatoshi Nagatomi and served as a Lecturer at McMaster University from around 1977 to 2003.

Grafton Elliot Smith (1871–1937) was an archaeologist and medical scholar. He studied at Sydney Medical School, the University of Sydney, and St John's College, and later held a post at University College London from around 1919 to 1936.

Graham E. Clarke (died 1998) worked in Tibetology and development studies. He held posts at the Institute of Development Studies and the University of Oxford, where he was attested as a Senior Member in 1998.
Graham Lock is a scholar of Buddhist studies and linguistics who studied under teachers Hsuan Hua and Saddhaloka Bhikkhu.

Graham Parkes (born 1949) earned his Ph.D. at UC Berkeley (~1974–1978). He served as Professor of Philosophy at the University of Hawaiʻi (~1991–2008) and later held multiple professorial and leadership roles at University College Cork (~2008–2013).

Graham Priest (born 1948) is a philosopher and Buddhist studies scholar who earned his PhD at the London School of Economics under John Lane Bell. His posts include professorships at the University of Melbourne and the CUNY Graduate Center.

Graves Chamney Haughton (1788–1849) studied at Fort William College before serving as Professor at the East India Company College (1819–1827), succeeding Alexander Hamilton. A co-founder of the Royal Asiatic Society, he served as its secretary around 1831–1832.

Gray Tuttle completed his Ph.D. in Inner Asian Studies at Harvard University in 2002, advised by William C. Kirby, Leonard van der Kuijp, and Philip A. Kuhn. He later served as Associate Professor at Columbia University (attested 2008–2015).

Graziadio Isaia Ascoli (1829–1907) was an Italian linguist and Indologist. He served as a professor at the Accademia Scientifico-Letteraria di Milano from 1861 to 1902 and founded the journal Archivio Glottologico Italiano in 1873.

Greg Bailey is an Indologist who earned his PhD at the University of Melbourne in 1980, supervised by J. Durham and Madeleine Biardeau. He held posts at La Trobe University and was a visiting fellow at the University of Tübingen (1998).

Gregor Ahn (born 1958) studied at Copenhagen and Bonn, completing his PhD and Habilitation under Hans-Joachim Klimkeit. He taught at Münster and Tartu before becoming Professor of Comparative Religion at the University of Heidelberg in 1996.

Gregory Forgues is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He earned a Magister der Philosophie at the University of Vienna (attested 2011) under Helmut Tauscher, alongside receiving traditional instruction from Dzongsar Jamyang Khyentse, Namkhai Norbu, Tri Hai, and Chanmyay Sayadaw.

Gregory Max Seton is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He earned degrees from Naropa University and UC Santa Barbara, followed by a D.Phil from Wolfson College, Oxford (2015), supervised by Vesna Wallace and Alexis Sanderson.

Gregory Nagy (born 1942) is a scholar of linguistics and classics. He completed his undergraduate studies at Indiana University (~1958–1962), studied at Harvard University (~1962–1966), and began his academic post at Harvard around 1969.

Gregory P. A. Levine (born 1963) studied at Oberlin College and Princeton University. He took up a post around 2002 as Associate Professor of Japanese art, architecture, and Buddhist visual cultures at the University of California, Berkeley.
